blocks.text: 55+ manufactured-home parks in BC: named examples

This is a representative set, not a full list. Each park below was verified by name from a public source that states its age restriction. Pad rents and fees are listing-stated for one home on one date, not a park tariff, so confirm them with the park.
Westwood Estates — 8254 134 St, Surrey (Queen Mary Park Surrey)

MLS listings describe "WESTWOOD ESTATES, 55+ age restricted", a gated manufactured-home park; one listing states a pad rent of $935 per month including the land portion of property taxes, garbage pickup, sewer and water, and that large dogs are allowed with park approval.
Newton Mobile Home Park — 6571 King George Blvd, Surrey (West Newton)

A park directory describes it as an age-restricted (55+) manufactured-home community and a land-lease community with a total of 34 home sites; MLS listings for homes in the park describe a "quiet 55+ community", subject to park approval, with no strata fees. The directory's lot-rent range carries its own warning that lot rent can change without notice — confirm the current pad rent with the park.
Val Maria (Val Maria Manufactured Home Park) — 21163 Lougheed Highway, Maple Ridge (Southwest Maple Ridge)

MLS listings repeatedly describe "VAL MARIA, 55+ age restricted manufactured home park" / "55+ age restricted park"; one listing states a monthly pad rent of $601.90 including the land portion of property taxes, garbage pickup, sewer and water, with 2 small pets allowed — listing-stated for that home; pad rents vary by home and date in the listings checked, so confirm the figure for the specific site.
Pinecrest Mobile Home Park (Pinecrest MHP) — 12022 Pretty Road, Lake Country (Okanagan)
Cultus Lake Village — 3942 Columbia Valley Road, Cultus Lake (Fraser Valley, near Chilliwack)

A listing for a home in the park describes "Cultus Lake Village, a welcoming 55+ community" and a "family-owned and operated park for over 25 years", walking distance to Cultus Lake. Park size: UNCONFIRMED from the sources checked.
Pioneer Park — 27111 0 Ave, Langley / Aldergrove (Township of Langley)

A 55+ manufactured-home co-operative: MLS listings state "Pioneer Park is 55+", that a buyer must be accepted by the co-op and purchase co-op shares (one listing: $9,200, refunded upon sale) and pay monthly co-op fees ($510 in the same listing) rather than pad rent. Because the land is held through the co-operative, this is not a standard Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act pad tenancy — confirm the tenure documents with the co-op.
Sea Ridge Bays — 15875 20 Ave, Surrey (South Surrey / King George Corridor)

A 55+ manufactured-home community that is a bare-land strata: MLS property data records "Age Restricted 55+" in its bylaws restrictions, and listings state "Sea Ridge Bays is 55+", "NO PAD FEES", and that as a bare-land strata "YOU OWN THE LOT", with a monthly strata fee ($210 in the listings, including water) instead of pad rent. Strata law, not the park tenancy Act, is the frame here.

Check each park yourself. Breakaway Bays in South Surrey produced conflicting age claims in the sources, and Crispen Bays and Crestway Bays on King George Boulevard are listed as all-ages, so a park’s age label cannot be assumed from its city.
BC rules for park tenancies and 55+ parks
The governing statute is the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act (MHPTA)

It applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on; a home on land the owner also owns is dealt with through the land title system instead, and if a person rents both the home and the site from an owner, the Residential Tenancy Act — not the MHPTA — applies.
The 55+ rule in a park is a park designation, not a strata bylaw

The Province states the general rule for a designated 55-plus park: at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. Individual parks can state their occupancy rule more strictly in their own documents — one Aldergrove co-op listing states both occupants must be 55 — so the park's own tenancy agreement and rules are the operative document, not the strata age-bylaw regime (Strata Property Act ss. 123.1/123.2 applies to strata corporations, not to pad tenancies).
Buying in a park is an assignment, not a new tenancy

When a home in a park is sold, the buyer does not get a new tenancy — the existing pad tenancy agreement is assigned to the purchaser. Before the seller asks the park owner to consent, the seller must give the proposed purchaser a copy of any written part of the tenancy agreement and any written park rules that apply to the tenancy.
Park owner consent and the 10-day rule

assignment needs the park owner's prior written consent (or consent deemed given, or an order of the director). The request is made in writing on the approved form (RTB Form 10), the park owner must respond so the home owner receives the response by the 10th day after the request is received, and if there is no response by the end of the 10th day, consent is deemed to have been given; the park owner must not charge a fee or receive a benefit for giving consent. On assignment, the purchaser becomes the tenant of the park owner and assumes the rights and obligations under the Act and the tenancy agreement from the assignment date, on the same terms as before.
Pad rent increases — the allowable formula

a landlord may increase pad rent once every 12 months, with at least 3 full months' notice, and the increase is capped by formula — the inflation rate (the 12-month average change in the BC all-items Consumer Price Index) plus a proportional amount (the change in local government levies plus the change in regulated park utilities, divided by the number of manufactured home sites in the park). The formula is set in the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Regulation.
Park rules

park rules are part of the tenancy agreement; a rule is enforceable only if it applies to all tenants fairly, is clear enough for a reasonable tenant to follow, is properly noticed, and does not change a material term of the tenancy agreement. Since the April 30, 2024 regulation change, park rules can only be changed once a year and with three months' notice.
Park closure or redevelopment

a landlord converting all or a significant part of a park to a non-residential use, or to a residential use other than a manufactured home park, must have all necessary government permits and approvals in place before issuing notice, must give a 12-month notice to end tenancy, and must pay the tenant $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date; a tenant may move out early on at least 10 days' written notice, paying rent to the move-out date.
Registration of the home itself — the Manufactured Home Registry

a sale, transfer or purchase of a manufactured home is only effective if registered in the Manufactured Home Registry, the province's central register of manufactured home ownership, administered through BC Registries. On a sale, the original signed Bill of Sale and the Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership are filed through a qualified supplier (a lawyer or notary), and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale.
Property tax and the Home Owner Grant

a manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential property owners, and the assessed value does not include the value of the land when the home is in a manufactured home park not on reserve land, or on land privately owned by someone other than the home owner. A manufactured home occupied as a principal residence by its registered owner can qualify for the Home Owner Grant, applied for each year.
Municipal layer

there is no province-wide park zoning — each municipality zones manufactured home parks in its own bylaw — and some cities add a park-redevelopment policy on top of the Act; Surrey's Manufactured Home Park Policy brochure, for example, walks residents through the 12-month notice, permits-first and $20,000 compensation steps and names help organizations including the BC Manufactured Home Owners association and the Tenant Resource & Advisory Centre.

blocks.text: Condo buildings in How to Buy a Condo in BC
Researched Nov 1, 2026. Every fact carries its source. Anything no source states is marked UNCONFIRMED. No sold prices. There is no MLS sub-area for this guide and no single municipality").
Streets, schools and getting around How to Buy a Condo in BC

items.t: This is a province-wide topic, not a place: how buying a strata condominium works in British Columbia — the documents, the taxes, the rebates, the strata rules — for any city or sub-area in BC.

What "condo" means in BC law: a strata lot in a strata plan registered under the Strata Property Act — most often an apartment unit in a low-rise or tower, but the same legal form covers townhouses and bare-land strata lots. The buyer's ownership is the strata lot plus a share of the common property, governed by the strata corporation's bylaws and rules. The Province's strata hub is the starting point for buyers.

The two purchase streams this topic covers: (1) resale — an existing strata lot bought from its owner, with disclosure through the Form B; and (2) presale / new construction — a lot bought from a developer before or during construction, governed by the Real Estate Development Marketing Act (REDMA) disclosure regime instead of the Form B at the contract stage. The rules in mark which stream each rule belongs to.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect condo buyers in How to Buy a Condo in BC

items.t: Depreciation reports (s.94): Required for stratas with 5+ lots, renewed at least every five years. From July 1, 2027, owner-developers of new strata plans must help fund the first depreciation report (lesser of $5,000 + $200 per strata lot, or $30,000), payable by the first AGM.

Insurance: The strata insures the common property and the buildings as originally built; the Form B insurance summary (April 1, 2023 onward) discloses the policy and its deductibles, including water-damage deductibles that can be assessed back to an owner — the reason unit-owner (strata) insurance is standard advice.

PTT — first-time buyer exemption: Qualifying first-time buyers pay no PTT on the first $500,000 of a home worth up to $835,000 (maximum saving $8,000), with a partial exemption between $835,000 and $860,000 and none at $860,000 or more; eligibility requires Canadian citizenship or permanent residence, a BC residency/tax-filing test, and never having owned an interest in a principal residence anywhere in the world.

Disclosure statement first: A developer must give the buyer a disclosure statement filed with the BC Financial Services Authority setting out all material facts (layouts, estimated strata fees, developer background, common property) before the contract binds; a contract signed without the required disclosure may not be enforceable.

7-day rescission: The buyer may cancel within 7 days after the later of signing the purchase agreement and receiving/acknowledging the disclosure statement, with the deposit refunded. Deposits are held in trust by a law firm, notary or brokerage, not paid to the developer directly. Material changes after signing require an amended disclosure statement.

Assignments: Selling a presale contract before completion is an assignment of paper, not of property. Developers typically restrict it — consent usually required, fees commonly 1%–3% of the original price, and some contracts prohibit assignment until sell-out or prohibit public marketing. Read the assignment clause before signing; the BC flipping tax is a separate consideration on short holds.

Home Buyers' Plan (HBP): Up to $60,000 per person withdrawn from an RRSP for a first home, repayable over the HBP period. First Home Savings Account (FHSA). $8,000 of contribution room per year to a $40,000 lifetime limit, deductible going in and tax-free coming out for a qualifying first home. The two can be combined for the same purchase.

CMHC mortgage insurance: Required when the down payment is under 20% on a home priced $1.5M or less; CMHC states premium rates range from 0.6% to 4.5% of the total mortgage amount (smaller down payment = higher premium), and the premium may be added to the loan. Minimum down payment is 5% on the first $500,000 and 10% on the portion above.

Municipal layer — zoning, OCP and SSMUH vary by city: There is no province-wide multi-family zoning; each municipality's zoning bylaw and OCP govern where condos can be built, while the Province's Bill 44 SSMUH legislation required every local government to allow small-scale multi-unit housing (a suite/ADU, 3–4 units, or 6 units near frequent bus stops, depending on lot and location) in formerly single-detached zones by June 30, 2024, subject to granted extensions.

blocks.text: Good to know about How to Buy a Condo in BC

items.t: November 24, 2022 — rental and age bylaws reset. Bill 44 (Building and Strata Statutes Amendment Act, 2022) voided all residential rental-restriction bylaws, ended the Form J Rental Disclosure Statement regime, and confined age bylaws to 55+ (Strata Property Act ss.123.1/123.2).
April 1, 2023 — Form B insurance summary. Strata corporations must include a summary of insurance coverage on the Form B.
May 1, 2023 — wider 55+ exemptions. Younger spouses/partners, children under 19 in the resident's care, and adult children previously cared for by the resident were added to the exemption list.
November 1, 2023 — 10% CRF minimum. AGM budgets must contribute at least 10% of the operating fund to the CRF; developer initial CRF contributions for new stratas rose to 10% as well.

April 1, 2024 — PTT thresholds raised. The first-time buyer exemption ceiling moved to $835,000 (partial to $860,000) and the newly built home exemption to $1,100,000 (phasing out at $1,150,000), the thresholds still in effect in the sources checked.

June 30, 2024 — SSMUH deadline. Local governments had to have zoning updated for small-scale multi-unit housing; by September 16, 2024 the Province reported 172 of 188 local governments had adopted SSMUH bylaws for areas without an extension, with 21 governments granted extensions (Chilliwack partially, to December 31, 2030, for the Proper/Hazel Park area).

July 1, 2024 — depreciation reports tightened. Five-year renewal became mandatory; stratas formed before that date with no report face the July 1, 2026 (CRD/FVRD/Metro Vancouver) and July 1, 2027 (rest of BC) catch-up deadlines.

October 27, 2025 — more depreciation-report professionals. Additional qualified professionals (including professional licensees in engineering, architectural technologists and certified technicians) may provide depreciation reports and electrical planning reports, per OIC 187-25.

March 13, 2026 — FTHB GST rebate becomes law. Bill C-4 received Royal Assent (CRA, Excise and GST/HST News No. 122, April 2026), bringing the 100%-to-$1M GST rebate for first-time buyers of new homes into force for agreements on/after March 20, 2025 and before 2031.

December 15, 2024 (financing rule, still current) — insured-mortgage cap $1.5M. CMHC insurance requires the home price to be $1.5M or less and applies the 5%-on-first-$500,000 / 10%-on-the-rest minimum down payment structure.

Strata manufactured-home parks generally

where a park has been converted to strata, the homes sit on strata lots and the Strata Property Act document set (Form B, depreciation report, filed bylaws, 55+ as the only valid age bylaw under ss.123.1/123.2) governs instead of pad-tenancy assignment.
Pioneer Park — 27111 0 Ave, Aldergrove. A manufactured-home CO-OPERATIVE
— a third form: the buyer purchases the home plus co-op shares and must be accepted by the co-op. Not strata, not pad-rental, not a townhouse.
Streets, schools and getting around How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC

items.t: The two ownership forms the topic is built around: (1) you own the home and rent the pad (site) it sits on in a manufactured home park — the land is the park owner's; (2) you own both the home and the land it sits on.

Which law applies to which form: the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on; a home on land you own is dealt with through the land title system instead. Neither form is a townhouse strata — a townhouse purchase is governed by the Strata Property Act, a different statute with a different document set (Form B, depreciation report, filed bylaws).

Terminology: "manufactured home" is the legal term; "mobile home" is the everyday term. A manufactured home is factory-built to the CSA standard and registered in the Manufactured Home Registry — it is not the same product class as a site-built townhouse, and the registry/CSA-label rules in are what separate a registrable manufactured home from an unregistered unit.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect townhome buyers in How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC

items.t: Pad tenure and assignment — the core of a park purchase: When a home in a park is sold, the buyer does not get a new tenancy — the existing pad tenancy agreement is assigned to the purchaser. Before the seller asks the park owner to consent, the seller must give the proposed purchaser a copy of any written part of the tenancy agreement and any written park rules that apply.

Park owner consent and the 10-day rule: Assignment needs the park owner's prior written consent (or consent deemed given, or an order of the director), requested in writing on RTB Form 10; the park owner must respond so the home owner receives the response by the 10th day after the request is received, silence by the end of the 10th day means consent is deemed given, and the park owner must not charge a fee for giving consent. On assignment the purchaser becomes the tenant, assumes the rights and obligations under the Act and the agreement from the assignment date, and the agreement continues on the same terms.

Park rules: are part of the tenancy agreement; a landlord may change park rules only with 3 full months' notice, and a rule is enforceable only if it applies to all tenants fairly, is clear enough for a reasonable tenant to follow, is properly noticed, and does not change a material term of the tenancy agreement.

Pad rent increases — VERIFIED figures, formula only, NEVER a dollar figure: A landlord may increase pad rent once every 12 months, with at least 3 full months' notice, capped at the inflation rate (the 12-month average change in the BC all-items Consumer Price Index) plus a proportional amount (the change in local government levies plus the change in regulated park utilities, divided by the number of manufactured home sites in the park). No official source publishes a pad-rent DOLLAR figure for any park, and none is published here — any page stating a specific park's pad rent in dollars is stating a listing figure, not an official one.

Park closure or redevelopment: A landlord converting all or a significant part of a park must have all necessary government permits and approvals in place before issuing notice, must give 12 months' notice to end tenancy, and must pay the tenant $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date; a tenant may move out early on at least 10 days' written notice, paying rent to the move-out date.

Ownership registry: A sale, transfer or purchase of a manufactured home is only effective if registered in the Manufactured Home Registry; on a sale, the original signed Bill of Sale and the Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership are filed through a qualified supplier (a lawyer or notary), and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale. There is no Form B in this system — the registry record and the tenancy agreement are the disclosure set.

Property tax: A manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential property owners, and the assessed value does not include the value of the land when the home is in a manufactured home park not on reserve land, or on land privately owned by someone other than the home owner. A manufactured home occupied as a principal residence by its registered owner can qualify for the Home Owner Grant, applied for each year.

Age-restricted parks: In a designated 55-plus park, at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older (the Province's general rule). That is a park rule under tenancy law — not a Strata Property Act s.123.1/123.2 bylaw — so the strata exemptions for younger spouses/partners, caregivers and defined children do not automatically apply inside a pad-rental park; the park rules govern.

Zoning for parks is municipal: There is no province-wide park zoning — for example, Surrey's Zoning Bylaw No. 12000 has a Manufactured Home Residential Zone (RM-M), and Maple Ridge's Zoning Bylaw 7600-2019 has an RMH Manufactured Home Park Residential zone.

Financing: lender and mortgage-insurer rules for manufactured homes (chattel vs land-home treatment, age and foundation requirements) were not confirmed on an official source in the research pass: UNVERIFIED — confirm financing terms for the specific home and tenure before removing subjects.
None of that machinery exists in a pad assignment — which is the point of the contrast.

blocks.text: Good to know about How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC

items.t: The consent clock is the park equivalent of a subject period, and most buyers have never heard of it: the park owner has 10 days to respond to an assignment request on RTB Form 10, and silence is consent — a deal structured without that window in its dates is structured wrong.
Two parks in the same city can post different lawful increases in the same year, and neither increase can be checked against a published dollar figure, because none exists on an official source.

A missing CSA label is a financing and resale problem, not a cosmetic one: the transfer only takes effect when registered, the filing goes through a lawyer or notary, and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale.

The tax assessment quietly tells you the tenure: in a park, the assessed value does not include the land, because the home owner does not own it — the cleanest one-line test of pad tenure on a tax notice, and the reason a park home and a townhouse at the same sticker figure are not the same asset.

Park rules can change on 3 months' notice; strata bylaws cannot change that way: a landlord may change park rules with 3 full months' notice (subject to the fairness/clarity/material-term limits), while a strata bylaw change needs an owner vote and Land Title filing. The daily-life rules of a park home are less locked-in than a townhouse buyer's.

blocks.text: Lots and land in How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC

states plainly that it carries NO land stock of its own. Its land content is the three ways a manufactured-home buyer holds ground — pad rental, bare-land strata lot, and fee-simple land — because for this topic the land question IS the purchase: two buyers can buy physically identical homes and own completely different things underneath them.

items.t: The buyer owns the manufactured home and rents the site under a pad tenancy agreement; the land is the park owner's, and the MHPTA is the governing statute. There is no land title, no strata lot and no Form B in this form.

On a sale, the buyer does not get a new tenancy — the existing pad tenancy agreement is ASSIGNED to the purchaser, with the park owner's prior written consent (RTB Form 10; response by the 10th day or consent is deemed given; no fee may be charged for consent). Before consent is even requested, the seller must give the proposed purchaser the written tenancy agreement and the written park rules.

Pad rent rises by formula, once every 12 months on at least 3 full months' notice: the inflation rate (BC all-items CPI) plus a proportional amount (the park's change in local government levies plus regulated park utilities, divided by the number of sites).

The ground risk in this form is the park's future: conversion of all or a significant part of a park requires all permits/approvals in place first, 12 months' notice, and $20,000 compensation payable on or before the notice's effective date.

Tax follows the split: a manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential owners, but the assessed value does NOT include the land's value when the home is in a park not on reserve land, or on land privately owned by someone other than the home owner.

In a bare-land strata, the buyer owns a strata lot and the manufactured home sits on land the buyer owns as that lot. Strata law — not the MHPTA — is the frame: Form B, monthly strata fees and registered bylaws apply TO THE LOT, and there is no pad rent.
Named precedent — Sea Ridge Bays, 15875 20 Ave, Surrey (South Surrey)

Age rule note: the only valid strata age bylaws are 55+ bylaws (Strata Property Act ss. 123.1/123.2, with the May 1, 2023 exemptions) — which is why a 55+ bare-land strata like Sea Ridge Bays is a lawful form, while a pad-rental park's 55+ rule is a park designation rule instead (at least one tenant on the site must be 55 or older, per the Province). Two different statutes produce a similar-looking "55+" label: do not merge them.

The buyer owns both the home and the land on a fee-simple title, dealt with through the land title system. There is no pad rent, no park owner and no strata — municipal zoning, building/siting rules and title charges govern the land, and the home itself must still satisfy the registry/CSA requirements in to be a registrable manufactured home.

Siting/CSA position, stated at the level the sources support: the home must carry its CSA certification label at the point of sale and the transfer is only effective when registered in the Manufactured Home Registry (filing through a lawyer or notary: original signed Bill of Sale + Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership). Municipal siting, foundation and permit requirements for placing a manufactured home on fee-simple land vary by municipality and are UNCONFIRMED at topic level — confirm with the municipality for the specific parcel.

Tax in this form: the home is taxed as an improvement on land the owner holds (the park exclusion in (a) does not apply), and a manufactured home occupied as a principal residence by its registered owner can qualify for the Home Owner Grant, applied for annually.

items.t: Which law applies follows the ground, not the home: the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act (MHPTA) applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on; a home on land you own is dealt with through the land title system instead, and a bare-land strata lot is governed by the Strata Property Act.

Terminology: a manufactured home is factory-built to the CSA standard and registered in the Manufactured Home Registry; the registry/CSA-label rules in are what separate a registrable manufactured home from an unregistered unit.
No figure is substituted.

Zoning for the ground is municipal, not provincial: there is no province-wide park zoning — for example, Surrey's Zoning Bylaw No. 12000 has a Manufactured Home Residential Zone (RM-M) permitting manufactured home parks, and Maple Ridge's Zoning Bylaw 7600-2019 has an RMH Manufactured Home Park Residential zone.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect land buyers in How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC

items.t: Registry first, all three forms: A sale, transfer or purchase of a manufactured home is only effective if registered in the Manufactured Home Registry; the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale. A missing label is a red flag for financing and resale in every form.

Pad-form rules (form (a) only): Park rules are part of the tenancy agreement; a landlord may change them only with 3 full months' notice, and a rule is enforceable only if it applies fairly to all tenants, is clear, is properly noticed and does not change a material term. On assignment the purchaser steps into the agreement on the same terms from the assignment date.

Strata-form rules (form (b) only) — the BC strata block: Form B Information Certificate (fees, amounts owed, approved levies, CRF balance, insurance summary; within 7 days, maximum $35 plus up to 25 cents per page); depreciation reports every 5 years for stratas with 5+ lots since July 1, 2024; minimum 10% CRF contribution since November 1, 2023; rental-restriction bylaws VOID since November 24, 2022; only 55+ age bylaws valid (SPA ss. 123.1/123.2, May 1, 2023 exemptions). A bare-land strata lot with a clubhouse/serviced common property carries exactly the assets a depreciation report prices — ask for the current one.

Fee-simple-form rules (form (c) only): No strata documents and no pad tenancy: zoning (municipal), siting/permit rules and title govern. Where the land is in the ALR, the ALR block also applies: residences cannot be stratified (ALC Bulletin 09 s. 6; SPA s. 239; ALCA s. 21(1)); subdivision within the ALR requires ALC approval; principal residence ≤500 m², suite within the principal residence only, additional residence 90 m² (≤40 ha) / 186 m² (>40 ha). BC Assessment farm class, full three-tier form: $2,500 (0.8–4 ha); $2,500 plus 5% of the actual value of the area over 4 ha (>4 ha); $10,000 (<0.8 ha); applications by October 31 — a flat "$2,500+" statement is an error.

Property transfer tax — stated ONLY at the level the BC source supports: The Province's newly built home exemption from PTT expressly includes "a manufactured home that is placed and affixed on a parcel of vacant land" (not previously occupied) as a newly built home — relevant to form (c) buyers placing a NEW manufactured home on their own land (full relief to $1,100,000, partial to $1,150,000 under that exemption). For a RESALE home on a rented pad (form (a)), the purchase is of the home and an assigned tenancy, not a registered transfer of land: at exactly that level, it is generally not a PTT transaction on land. Finer points — bare-land strata lot transfers (form (b), which DO transfer a registered strata lot), partial interests, and any specific transaction's treatment — are UNCONFIRMED here and must be confirmed against the BC PTT guidance / a lawyer before writing.

GST — stated ONLY at the level CRA sources support: For the land forms: the CRA treats most individuals' sales of vacant land kept for personal use as exempt, with taxable examples including land used primarily in a business, land sold in the course of a business, and parcels created by subdividing into more than two parts — directly relevant to a form (c) lot bought from a subdivider vs an individual. The FTHB GST rebate (Bill C-4, Royal Assent March 13, 2026, CRA News No. 122; 100% to $1M, maximum $50,000, phasing to $1.5M, agreements Mar 20, 2025–2031) applies to new HOUSING, not bare land itself; whether a new manufactured home placed on owned land qualifies is transaction-specific: UNCONFIRMED per transaction. New Housing Rebate: 36% / maximum $6,300 / $350,000–$450,000 phase-out.

Speculation/vacancy taxes + federal prohibition — topic level: Both turn on the specific municipality, property class and buyer status, and this topic has no single area: no area position is imported here. A fee-simple or bare-land strata home in a designated BC speculation and vacancy tax area (e.g., Surrey, Township of Langley) carries the annual declaration; a pad-form home's position differs again. Confirm for the specific property/municipality — UNCONFIRMED at topic level beyond that statement. Vancouver's Empty Homes Tax (3%) is Vancouver ONLY.

Financing: Lender and mortgage-insurer rules for manufactured homes (chattel vs land-home treatment, age and foundation requirements) were not confirmed on an official source in the research pass: UNCONFIRMED — confirm financing for the specific home AND its ground form before removing subjects; the same home can finance differently in forms (a), (b) and (c).

Zoning/siting for placing a home: Municipal only: parks sit in park zones (e.g., Surrey RM-M; Maple Ridge RMH); placing a manufactured home on fee-simple land is governed by that municipality's zoning and siting rules — no province-wide designation exists and none is asserted.

items.t: The consent clock is the deal clock in a park purchase. Ten days, in writing, on RTB Form 10 — and silence works FOR the buyer (deemed consent). Subject dates written without that window are written wrong.
And neither park's increase can be checked against a published dollar rent, because none exists on an official source.

"You own the lot" is the single most valuable sentence in this topic — and it only appears in one form. Sea Ridge Bays' listing language ("NO PAD FEES… YOU OWN THE LOT") exists precisely because pad buyers do not own their ground. When a listing for any manufactured home does not say which of the three forms it is, that omission is the first question, before price.

Claims / page-statement check for this topic. The owner-approved claims (REALTOR since 2015; 10 straight years in the FVREB Medallion Club; Top 1% of Fraser Valley Realtors; #1 in South Surrey/White Rock by MLS points for 2025 and 2026 YTD; more than $500M in sales) may be used only as page statements in that exact form. blocks.text: How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC: how mobile and manufactured homes work here
The parks and the homes

items.t: A home on a rented pad is not land ownership: In a pad-rental park the buyer owns the home — a chattel, registered in the Manufactured Home Registry — and rents the pad from the park owner under a Manufactured Home Site Tenancy Agreement. There is no land title, no strata lot and no Form B in this form.

Own-land manufactured-home stock is a different stock: In a bare-land strata park the buyer owns the lot as a strata lot — Form B, strata fees and registered bylaws apply, and there is no pad rent. In a co-operative the land is held through the co-op and the buyer holds a co-op interest plus the home. On fee-simple land the buyer owns the parcel outright.

blocks.text: Scope and area context

items.t: The two ownership forms the guide is built around: (1) you own the home and rent the pad (site) it sits on in a manufactured home park — the land is the park owner's; (2) you own both the home and the land it sits on.

Zoning for parks is municipal, not provincial: there is no province-wide park zoning — each municipality zones manufactured home parks in its own bylaw; for example, Surrey's Zoning Bylaw No. 12000 has a Manufactured Home Residential Zone (RM-M) permitting manufactured home parks, and Maple Ridge's Zoning Bylaw 7600-2019 has an RMH Manufactured Home Park Residential zone.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect park-home buyers

items.t: Pad rent increases: A landlord may increase pad rent once every 12 months, with at least 3 full months' written notice, capped by formula — the inflation rate (the 12-month average change in the BC all-items Consumer Price Index) plus a proportional amount (the change in local government levies plus the change in regulated park utilities, divided by the number of manufactured home sites in the park); the landlord may not round up and may not carry forward an unused portion of a prior year's limit. The caps verified live from the RTB (Nov 1, 2026): 2026 = 2.3% + proportional amount; 2027 = 2.2% + proportional amount.

Age rules in parks are park designations, not strata bylaws: The Province states the general rule for a designated 55-plus park: at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. Individual parks can state their occupancy rule more strictly in their own documents, so the park's own tenancy agreement and rules are the operative document.

Municipal layer on top of the Act: Some cities add a park-redevelopment policy on top of the MHPTA; Surrey's Manufactured Home Park Policy brochure, for example, walks residents through the 12-month notice, permits-first and $20,000 compensation steps and names help organizations including the BC Manufactured Home Owners association and the Tenant Resource & Advisory Centre.

blocks.text: Good to know

items.t: June 6, 2018: The Province's information bulletin states the new compensation for tenants of manufactured home parks facing eviction took effect June 6, 2018: compensation on a park closure/conversion became a flat $20,000, increased from the previous requirement of 12 months of pad rental costs; the same changes require park owners to compensate tenants for the assessed value of the home over $20,000 where the manufactured home cannot be relocated, clarify that a tenant unable to relocate the home is not responsible for disposal costs, and set bad-faith closure compensation at 12 months' pad rental or $5,000, whichever is greater.

2019: The Province's September 4, 2019 release states rent increase limits are tied only to the inflation rate (the 12-month average percentage change in the BC Consumer Price Index), and that for manufactured home park tenancies the rate is that inflation figure plus a proportional amount for changes in local government levies and regulated utility fees — the formula structure still in use, whose verified outputs are 2.3% + proportional (2026) and 2.2% + proportional (2027).

April 30, 2024: The Province announced April 30, 2024 that changes to the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Regulation mean park owners may change park rules only once per year, must give tenants three months' notice of a rule change (up from two weeks), and must give that notice on a form approved by the Residential Tenancy Branch.

October 20, 2025: Surrey adopted its Tenant Protection Bylaw No. 21788 and Rental Replacement Policy No. O-63 on October 20, 2025 for multi-unit rental redevelopment, and the bylaw does not apply to property governed by the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act — a dated reminder that park residents' redevelopment protection remains the provincial 12-month notice and $20,000 framework plus any city park policy, not the new city bylaw.

blocks.text: The rules for buying in a park
Pad tenancy, park-owner consent, pad-rent caps and the Manufactured Home Registry are explained on their own page.

items.t: BC mobile home buying rules

faq.q: If I buy a mobile home in a park, do I own the land?
faq.a: No. You own the home and rent the site under a pad tenancy agreement; the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on.

faq.q: Can the park owner refuse to let me buy a home in the park?
faq.a: The sale needs the park owner's prior written consent to assign the tenancy — but the owner must respond within 10 days of the written request, silence counts as consent given, no fee can be charged for consent, and if consent is unreasonably withheld the home owner can apply for dispute resolution.

faq.q: How much can my pad rent go up each year?
faq.a: Once every 12 months, on at least 3 full months' notice, by no more than the inflation rate (BC consumer price index) plus a proportional amount for the park's changes in local government levies and regulated utilities, divided by the number of sites in the park.

faq.q: What happens to me if the park is sold or redeveloped?
faq.a: For a conversion of all or a significant part of the park, the landlord must have all permits and approvals first, give 12 months' notice, and pay you $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date.

faq.q: How is the purchase actually registered?
faq.a: Through the Manufactured Home Registry — the sale is only effective once registered. Your lawyer or notary files the original signed Bill of Sale and the Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership, and the home must carry its CSA certification label at the point of sale.

faq.q: If I buy a mobile home in a park, do I own the land?
faq.a: No — in a pad-rental park you own the home and rent the site under a pad tenancy agreement; the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on. The exceptions in prove the rule: in a bare-land strata park such as Sea Ridge Bays you own the lot as a strata lot, and in a co-operative such as Pioneer Park the land is held through the co-op.

faq.q: How is financing different for a home on a rented pad?
faq.a: The home is registered in the Manufactured Home Registry rather than dealt with as land title real property, and the transfer is only effective once registered, filed through a lawyer or notary with the signed Bill of Sale and Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership. Lender and mortgage-insurer rules for manufactured homes (chattel vs land-home treatment, age and foundation requirements) were not confirmed on an official source in this research — UNCONFIRMED; confirm financing for the specific home and tenure before removing subjects, and note the extreme case in the Surrey research: a membership (non-strata, non-park) complex whose listing states no mortgages are possible at all.

faq.q: Can the park owner refuse to let me buy a home in the park?
faq.a: The sale needs the park owner's prior written consent to assign the tenancy — but the owner must respond within 10 days of the written request (RTB Form 10), silence counts as consent given, and no fee can be charged for consent. Listings phrase this as "subject to park approval".

faq.q: How much can my pad rent go up each year?
faq.a: Once every 12 months, on at least 3 full months' notice, by no more than the inflation rate (BC consumer price index) plus a proportional amount for the park's changes in local government levies and regulated utilities, divided by the number of sites in the park. For scale, the RTB's own rent-increase form for manufactured home sites states the formula outcome as 3% plus the proportional amount for increases effective in 2025, and 2.3% plus the proportional amount for increases effective in 2026.

faq.q: Can I move my home to another park later?
faq.a: The Act's framework assumes a home can be relocated — the closure-compensation rules even add compensation where a home cannot be moved — but the practical answer depends on the home's age, condition, CSA label and whether another park will accept it, none of which an official source guarantees: UNCONFIRMED for any specific home. What is fixed in law is the paperwork: any later sale or transfer is only effective once registered in the Manufactured Home Registry, and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale — a missing label is a red flag for moving, financing and resale.

faq.q: What happens if the park is sold or redeveloped?
faq.a: A sale of the park alone does not end your tenancy — your assigned tenancy continues on the same terms. A conversion of all or a significant part of the park is different: the landlord must have all permits and approvals first, give 12 months' notice, and pay you $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date; you may leave early on at least 10 days' written notice.

faq.q: Is a park's 55+ age restriction legally valid?
faq.a: Yes, as a park designation under the provincial framework: the Province states that in a designated 55-plus park at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. This is a different legal mechanism from a strata's 55+ bylaw — do not apply strata exemption rules to a pad tenancy; read the park's tenancy agreement and rules, which can state the occupancy rule more strictly.

faq.q: What paperwork should the seller hand me before I write an offer?
faq.a: The written tenancy agreement and the written park rules — the regulation requires the seller to give the proposed purchaser both before the park owner is even asked to consent to the assignment — plus the current pad rent and the date of the last increase, so the increase formula can be checked.

faq.q: Do I pay property tax on a home I own on a rented pad?
faq.a: Yes — a manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential property owners, but the assessed value does not include the value of the land when the home is in a manufactured home park not on reserve land. Some parks include the land portion of property taxes inside the pad rent (Westwood Estates and Val Maria listings both state this) — check what the specific park's pad rent includes.

faq.q: A directory calls a park 55+, but a listing in it says no age restrictions. Which is right?
faq.a: Treat the park as UNCONFIRMED until its own rules settle it — that exact conflict occurred in this research at Breakaway Bays in South Surrey (directory: 55+; MLS listing: "No age or rental restrictions"). Ask the park for its current tenancy agreement and park rules in writing before relying on either claim.

faq.q: What documents should I read before removing subjects on a resale condo?
faq.a: The Form B with its attachments — current budget, bylaws and rules, and the most recent depreciation report — plus at least two years of strata council and AGM minutes. The Form B is a prescribed certificate under s.59 of the Strata Property Act and must include the insurance summary since April 1, 2023.

faq.q: What do strata fees actually cover, and what is the CRF?
faq.a: Fees split between the operating fund (day-to-day common expenses) and the contingency reserve fund (major repairs that occur less than yearly). Since November 1, 2023 at least 10% of the operating fund must go to the CRF each year. A low fee with a thin CRF and an old depreciation report is how special levies happen.

faq.q: Can the strata stop me renting out my condo?
faq.a: Not long-term — rental-restriction bylaws have been void since November 24, 2022. It can still restrict short-term rentals, and an age bylaw (55+) can restrict who may live there, tenant or owner.

faq.q: Can I buy in a 55+ building if I'm 48 and my partner is 57?
faq.a: Ownership is not age-restricted, and residence is permitted where a resident meets the age requirement — with the May 1, 2023 exemptions expressly covering a younger spouse or partner of a qualifying resident. Check the specific bylaw wording.

faq.q: Are pets and parking guaranteed by the listing?
faq.a: No. Pet bylaws are building-specific and survive in the filed bylaws; parking and storage entitlements for the specific lot are stated on the Form B (stall/locker numbers or "none"), not in listing copy. Directory and listing pet lines are leads, not proof.

faq.q: The listing calls this park home a "townhouse." Is it one?
faq.a: A townhouse is a strata lot (or a fee-simple row home) under land-title law.

faq.q: What replaces the Form B and depreciation report when I buy in a park?
faq.a: Nothing equivalent — the disclosure set is the written tenancy agreement and park rules (which the seller must give you before consent is even requested), the Manufactured Home Registry record, and the home's CSA certification label, which must be attached at the point of sale. That thinner disclosure is a real difference from a townhouse strata purchase, not a technicality.

faq.q: What is a bare-land strata lot, in one sentence?
faq.a: A strata lot that is land rather than a built unit: you own the lot, pay strata fees instead of pad rent, and get the strata document set (Form B, bylaws, depreciation report) for the lot.

faq.q: How much is pad rent?
faq.a: Get the current pad rent from the park's written Manufactured Home Site Tenancy Agreement for the specific home, never from a web range.
